title: Pandas Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Pandas lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Build a DataFrame
entries.summary: A DataFrame is a table with labelled columns and rows. Each list supplied here becomes one column.

example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Asha", "Ben", "Cara"],
    "score": [8, 6, 9],
    "team": ["red", "blue", "red"]
})

print(df.shape)

notes: All column lists must have compatible lengths when building this table.

entries.name: Select a column
entries.summary: Selecting one column by name returns a Series. A Series is a labelled one-dimensional set of values.

example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Asha", "Ben", "Cara"],
    "score": [8, 6, 9],
    "team": ["red", "blue", "red"]
})

print(df["score"].tolist())

notes: A misspelled column name raises an error rather than guessing your meaning.

entries.name: Read by label with loc
entries.summary: loc selects using row and column labels. This table has default row labels 0, 1 and 2.

example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Asha", "Ben", "Cara"],
    "score": [8, 6, 9],
    "team": ["red", "blue", "red"]
})

print(df.loc[1, "name"])

notes: A row label is not always the same as its position after the index changes.

entries.name: Read by position with iloc
entries.summary: iloc selects by zero-based positions. Its row and column numbers describe where values are placed.

example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Asha", "Ben", "Cara"],
    "score": [8, 6, 9],
    "team": ["red", "blue", "red"]
})

print(df.iloc[0, 1])

notes: Do not pass a column name to iloc when it expects a position.

entries.name: Filter rows
entries.summary: A condition creates a true-or-false value for each row. Use that condition to keep matching rows.

example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Asha", "Ben", "Cara"],
    "score": [8, 6, 9],
    "team": ["red", "blue", "red"]
})

passed = df[df["score"] >= 8]
print(passed["name"].tolist())

notes: Be explicit about whether the boundary value is included.

entries.name: Add a calculated column
entries.summary: A new column can come from a calculation on an existing one. Matching rows keep their relationship.

example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Asha", "Ben", "Cara"],
    "score": [8, 6, 9],
    "team": ["red", "blue", "red"]
})

df["bonus_score"] = df["score"] + 1
print(df["bonus_score"].tolist())

notes: Keep the original column when you still need the unmodified data.

entries.name: Sort rows by a value
entries.summary: sort_values orders rows by a selected column. The other columns move with their row so names and scores stay matched.

example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Asha", "Ben", "Cara"],
    "score": [8, 6, 9],
    "team": ["red", "blue", "red"]
})

ordered = df.sort_values("score")
print(ordered["name"].tolist())

notes: Do not sort each column separately; that breaks row relationships.

entries.name: Handle missing values
entries.summary: A missing value means data is absent. isna identifies missing entries; filling them requires a justified choice.

example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Asha", "Ben", "Cara"],
    "score": [8, 6, 9],
    "team": ["red", "blue", "red"]
})

values = pd.Series([2.0, None, 6.0])
print(values.isna().tolist())

notes: Do not replace every missing value with zero unless zero has the right meaning.

entries.name: Group and summarise
entries.summary: groupby gathers rows with the same key. An aggregation, such as mean, gives one summary for each group.

example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Asha", "Ben", "Cara"],
    "score": [8, 6, 9],
    "team": ["red", "blue", "red"]
})

means = df.groupby("team")["score"].mean()
print(float(means.loc["red"]))

notes: A small group's average can be unstable; keep its size in mind.

entries.name: Join related tables
entries.summary: merge combines tables using shared keys. Check whether each key is unique before deciding how the join should behave.

example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Asha", "Ben", "Cara"],
    "score": [8, 6, 9],
    "team": ["red", "blue", "red"]
})

teams = pd.DataFrame({"team": ["red", "blue"], "room": ["A", "B"]})
joined = df.merge(teams, on="team", validate="many_to_one")
print(joined.loc[joined["name"] == "Ben", "room"].iloc[0])

notes: Duplicate keys can multiply rows; validate the relationship you expect.

entries.name: Read a tiny CSV
entries.summary: CSV stores rows as text separated by commas. read_csv can read it from a file or, here, an in-memory text buffer.

example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Asha", "Ben", "Cara"],
    "score": [8, 6, 9],
    "team": ["red", "blue", "red"]
})

from io import StringIO
small = pd.read_csv(StringIO("item,count\nbook,2\npen,3\n"))
print(small["count"].sum())

notes: Check inferred data types and missing values after reading a real file.

entries.name: Copy a selected table before changing it
entries.summary: Make your intended copy explicit when you want to edit a subset independently. This keeps the original table easier to reason about.

example.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Asha", "Ben", "Cara"],
    "score": [8, 6, 9],
    "team": ["red", "blue", "red"]
})

selected = df.loc[df["team"] == "red"].copy()
selected["score"] = 0
print(df["score"].tolist())

notes: Avoid chained assignment; use clear loc assignment or an explicit copy.
